newsitem.title: USA: Calif. welfare ruling no threat to $900 mln - Gov..
newsitem.headline: Calif. welfare ruling no threat to $900 mln - Gov..

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson said on Wednesday that a recent state Supreme Court ruling does not threaten nearly $900 million of state funding for county health care programs.
"A fiscal crisis for counties has been averted for now and counties will continue to receive funds for their indigent health care services," Wilson, a Republican, said in a statement.

In March, the California state Supreme Court ruled that San Diego County may receive repayment for certain welfare costs. Attorneys involved in the case said the ruling could open the door for other counties to seek reimbursement.
The Supreme Court directed California's Commission on State Mandates to determine what, if any, funds are owed to San Diego County as a result of the ruling.
At the time, the Wilson administration warned that the ruling could activate so-called "poison pill" language in 1991 state legislation.
That "poison pill" provision would shut off vehicle license fee revenues used by counties to pay for health care services for poor adults on welfare.

Following the ruling, H.D. Palmer, a spokesman for the state's Department of Finance, warned that the "poison pill," if triggered, would cut off nearly $900 million in funds to counties in the 1997-1998 fiscal year alone.
In his statement Wednesday, Wilson said the "poison pill" would not be triggered as counties had feared.
"When the Supreme Court issued its ruling last month, I said that we would take a thorough and thoughtful review of the legal, fiscal, and policy issues that it raised," he said.
"We've completed that review, and we have determined that in this specific case, the court's ruling does not trigger the 'poison pill' language at this time," Wilson said.
"This is the result we were expecting," said Moody's Investors Service Inc vice president David Brodsly.
Had the "poison pill" been activited, Brodsly said counties would certainly have been hurt. "$900 million is a significant number for county government," he said.
